newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: ETHNIC HUNGARIANS PROTEST SLOVAK-ONLY REPORT CARDS.
newsitem.headline: ETHNIC HUNGARIANS PROTEST SLOVAK-ONLY REPORT CARDS.

text.p: Many ethnic Hungarian pupils in Slovakia refused to accept their year-end report cards on Friday because they were written in only Slovak instead of traditional bilingual reports.

The move to reject the Slovak-only reports was a protest against what the ethnic Hungarians consider to be a violation of their basic rights by the government of Premier Vladimir Meciar, leaders of the ethnic Hungarian community said.
"A more than 77-year long tradition of bilingual reports has been broken," Bela Bugar, leader of the ethnic Hungarian Christian Democrats Party, told the independent radio Twist.

"The current regime is behaving even worse than that of (Jozef) Tiso... which tolerated bilingual reports," Bugar, an opposition member of parliament said, referring to the president of 1939-1945 Slovak Nazi-puppet state.
The official Slovak news agency TASR reported that many ethnic Hungarian students in various spots in the south of the country had joined in the protest.
The Slovak Education Ministry ordered only Slovak-language reports to be issued in elementary and secondary schools.
The directive applied also to schools in southern Slovakia where most of the 600,000-strong ethnic Hungarian minority live, many of which use Hungarian as a teaching language.
The ministry, in this country of roughly five million people, based its decision on a 1995 state language law.

"The issue of single-language reports in Hungarian- language schools... is strictly according the law which says all official documents must be in the state language," Gejza Sadecky head of the ministry's school department told TASR.
Many parents refused to send their children to school in protest against the move, while several Hungarian language schools administrators disobeyed official orders and issued bilingual reports.
Meciar's ruling coalition accused ethnic Hungarian politicians of inflating the issue.
"They would accept the reports if they were written only in Hungarian," said Jan Cuper legal spokesman of Meciar's Movement for a Democratic Slovakia (HZDS).
"I pray this will not happen in my lifetime," Cuper added.

Anna Malikova, the vice-chairwoman of the far-right Slovak National Party (SNS) which holds the education ministry portfolio said that barring children from attending school on Friday was "blatent abuse of children".
"Why are Hungarian politicians playing this dangerous game with fire," she asked.

Slovakia has been battered by criticism from the European Union and the United States which have said the that Bratislava government has been dragging its feet on democratic reforms and improving its treatment of the country's ethnic minorites.
Earlier this week, the EU called on Slovakia to withdraw a school handbook published with EU-financing which disclaims the persecution of Slovak Jews during World War Two.
Meciar, attending an EU conference on Friday in Amsterdam on Friday, rejected the calls but agreed that it would not be used as a textbook in Slovak schools.
